clues.clue: This CB1 neighborhood was an independent city before being annexed by the City of Brooklyn in 1855; its name honors engineer Jonathan Williams.
clues.reveal: Williamsburg (CB1). An independent city until Brooklyn annexed it in 1855; named for engineer Jonathan Williams.

clues.clue: CB11's Bensonhurst takes its name from the family that owned the farmland here before it was developed in the 1880s.
clues.reveal: Benson (CB11, Bensonhurst). Named for the family that farmed the land before 1880s development.

clues.clue: Developed by Charles S. Brown in the late 1800s, this CB16 neighborhood became a densely populated Jewish immigrant community in the early 20th century.
clues.reveal: Brownsville (CB16). Developed by Charles S. Brown; a major Jewish immigrant community by the early 1900s.

clues.clue: East New York (CB5) was founded in the 1830s by John Pitkin, a merchant from this New England state who hoped to rival Manhattan.
clues.reveal: Connecticut (CB5, East New York). Founder John Pitkin came from Connecticut and hoped to rival Manhattan.

clues.clue: This CB9 neighborhood and its preserved 18th-century Dutch farmhouse in Prospect Park both carry the name of an old Brooklyn family.
clues.reveal: Lefferts (CB9). Named for an old Dutch family whose 18th-century farmhouse is preserved in Prospect Park.

clues.clue: All of Brooklyn sits within this New York State county, whose name also appears on the borough's hospital and Supreme Court.
clues.reveal: Kings County. Brooklyn is coextensive with Kings County, named in 1683 for King Charles II of England. The borough has 18 community districts in all.

clues.clue: The current borough president, who certainly has a plan.
clues.reveal: Antonio Reynoso. Brooklyn's borough president since 2022 and the first Latino to hold the office; he has championed a comprehensive plan for the borough's growth.

clues.clue: Borough president from 2002 to 2013, this exuberant 'cheerleader' branded Brooklyn and helped bring Barclays Center.
clues.reveal: Marty Markowitz. Brooklyn borough president from 2002 to 2013, known for relentless boosterism and backing the Barclays Center.

clues.clue: Brooklyn's borough-wide chief prosecutor, the Kings County District Attorney first elected in his own right in 2017.
clues.reveal: Eric Gonzalez. The Kings County District Attorney, Brooklyn's borough-wide chief prosecutor, known for a conviction review unit and a focus on non-jail outcomes.

clues.clue: This borough president from 2014 to 2021, a former NYPD captain, went on to become Mayor of New York City.
clues.reveal: Eric Adams. Brooklyn borough president from 2014 to 2021 and a former NYPD captain; he served as the 111th Mayor of New York City from 2022 to 2025.

clues.clue: After losing the 1895 mayor's race to Wurster, this man became Brooklyn's very first borough president in 1898.
clues.reveal: Edward M. Grout. He lost the 1895 mayoral race to Wurster but became Brooklyn's first borough president in 1898 after consolidation.

clues.clue: The hardest one: before 1898, Brooklyn had its own mayor. Name the last man to hold that office, elected in 1896, whose job vanished at consolidation.
clues.reveal: Frederick W. Wurster. The last Mayor of the City of Brooklyn (1896 to 1897); the office was abolished when Brooklyn joined Greater New York in 1898 and was replaced by the borough president.

clues.clue: One of the six original towns of Kings County, this CB14 area was settled by the Dutch in 1651 as Midwout, meaning 'middle woods'.
clues.reveal: Flatbush (CB14). Settled by the Dutch in 1651 as Midwout; one of the six original towns of Kings County.

clues.clue: This CB18 neighborhood is named for the Lenape people who lived in the area; it was farmland and a fishing resort before 20th-century development.
clues.reveal: Canarsie (CB18). Named for the Lenape band who lived there; once farmland and a fishing resort.

clues.clue: This CB3 district holds one of the nation's largest collections of intact Victorian architecture; its hyphenated name joins Bedford with this Dutch-derived word.
clues.reveal: Bedford-Stuyvesant (CB3). Holds one of the largest stocks of intact Victorian rowhouses in the country.

clues.clue: In 1965 this CB2 neighborhood became New York City's first designated Historic District; its name pairs with 'Brooklyn'.
clues.reveal: Brooklyn Heights (CB2). Designated New York City's first Historic District in 1965.

clues.clue: Brooklynites call this 1898 event, when their city dissolved into Greater New York and became one of five boroughs, the 'Great Mistake'.
clues.reveal: Consolidation (1898). On January 1, 1898 Brooklyn ceased to be an independent city and became one of New York City's five boroughs. Many Brooklynites called it the 'Great Mistake of 1898'.

clues.clue: The name 'Brooklyn' evolved from this Dutch town, established by settlers in the 1640s.
clues.reveal: Breukelen. The borough's name comes from the Dutch town of Breukelen, settled in the 1640s on the shore of Long Island.

clues.clue: This CB6 canal, designated a federal Superfund site in 2010, was once a tidal creek used by the Lenape and Dutch settlers.
clues.reveal: Gowanus (CB6). A Lenape tidal creek, later a canal, named a federal Superfund site in 2010.

clues.clue: Industrialist Irving T. Bush built this massive Sunset Park (CB7) shipping and manufacturing complex on the waterfront in the early 1900s; today it is Industry City's neighbor.
clues.reveal: Bush Terminal (CB7, Sunset Park). Built by Irving T. Bush in the early 1900s; today the neighbor of Industry City.

clues.clue: Opened in 1964 from CB10's Bay Ridge to Staten Island, this was the world's longest suspension bridge at the time; it honors an Italian explorer.
clues.reveal: Verrazzano (CB10, Bay Ridge). The 1964 bridge to Staten Island, then the world's longest suspension span.

clues.clue: Designed by Olmsted and Vaux and running through CB12, this boulevard opened in 1880 and has the country's first dedicated bike path along it.
clues.reveal: Ocean Parkway (CB12). An Olmsted and Vaux boulevard, opened 1880, with the country's first dedicated bike path (1894).

clues.clue: CB17's East Flatbush is home to this county-named hospital center, one of the borough's largest public medical campuses.
clues.reveal: Kings (CB17, East Flatbush). Kings County Hospital Center, one of the borough's largest public medical campuses.

clues.clue: With more than 2.7 million residents, Brooklyn ranks first among New York City's boroughs by this measure.
clues.reveal: Population. Brooklyn is the most populous of New York City's five boroughs, with roughly 2.7 million residents across its 18 community districts.

clues.clue: By the late 1800s CB4's Bushwick was a national capital of this beverage industry, home to a stretch nicknamed 'Brewers' Row'.
clues.reveal: Brewing (CB4, Bushwick). A national beer capital in the 1800s, with a stretch known as Brewers' Row.

clues.clue: From 1913 to 1957 the Brooklyn Dodgers played at this ballpark in CB8's Crown Heights, later replaced by apartments.
clues.reveal: Ebbets Field (CB8). Home of the Brooklyn Dodgers from 1913 to 1957, later replaced by apartments.

clues.clue: Opened in 1927 in CB13's Coney Island and now a city landmark, this wooden roller coaster is among the most famous in the world.
clues.reveal: Cyclone (CB13, Coney Island). The 1927 wooden roller coaster, now a New York City landmark.

clues.clue: This CB15 bay and neighborhood are named for a local fish; the area was famous for seafood restaurants and a 19th-century racetrack.
clues.reveal: Sheepshead Bay (CB15). Named for a local fish; once known for seafood and a 19th-century racetrack.

clues.clue: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux considered this 526-acre Brooklyn park, opened in 1867, their masterpiece, greater than Central Park.
clues.reveal: Prospect Park (1867). The 526-acre park by Olmsted and Vaux, the same designers as Central Park, who reportedly considered Prospect Park their finest work.

clues.clue: Opened in 1883 after 14 years of work, this East River span linked Brooklyn to Manhattan and helped pave the way for consolidation.
clues.reveal: Brooklyn Bridge (1883). The East River crossing, once the world's longest suspension bridge, tied Brooklyn to Manhattan and accelerated the push toward consolidation.
